stories.title: U.S. Apartment Rents Post Eighth Consecutive Month of Growth
stories.excerpt: U.S. apartment rents were essentially flat in July, with the national average rising +0.03% to $1,747 from June’s upwardly revised level of $1,746, CoStar Group’s Apartments.com reported Wednesday. This marks the eighth consecutive month of positive rent increases following a period of flat to declining monthly performance in the second half of 2025. On an annual basis, rent growth accelerated to +1.0% in July 2026 from the upwardly revised +0.9% in June and was slightly down from the +1.1% reading recorded one year earlier. June 2026 was initially reported as a +0.1% month-over-month increase and has been revised upward to +0.2%. Although apartment rent growth typically slows as the market moves further into the summer leasing season, gains in July were particularly subdued. “Following modest rent increases during the spring, the +0.03% increase recorded in July represents a notable slowdown in monthly pricing momentum,” according to Apartments.com. “While annual rent growth continues to improve gradually, elevated supply levels continue to restrain pricing momentum nationally.” Where the apartment industry connects. Meet the owners, investors, developers, lenders, brokers, and service providers driving today’s multifamily market at Connect Apartments. Build relationships, uncover opportunities, and stay ahead of what’s next. The post U.S. Apartment Rents Post Eighth Consecutive Month of Growth appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: U.S. apartment rents +0.03% MoM in July; +1.0% YoY, eighth consecutive month of gains
Elevated national supply levels continue to restrain pricing momentum despite positive trajectory
Annual rent growth slowing from prior-year +1.1% reading; summer leasing season typically dampens gains
stories.summary: U.S. apartment rents rose just 0.03% month-over-month in July 2026, marking the eighth consecutive month of positive growth but representing a notable deceleration in pricing momentum. Year-over-year growth accelerated modestly to 1.0% from 0.9% in June, but remains below the 1.1% recorded one year prior. Apartments.com notes that elevated supply levels across the nation continue to constrain rent growth, even as the market shows steady if muted improvement.
stories.impact: Persistent national supply overhang is preventing meaningful rent acceleration despite eight months of consecutive gains. Developers should expect continued cap-rate pressure and heightened competition in markets with elevated pipeline activity; selective, supply-constrained submarkets (like coastal infill) will command premium pricing and absorption velocity advantages. New starts remain disciplined but conversion risk rises if lending tightens further.

stories.title: Costa Mesa Multifamily Changes Hands for Value-Add Repositioning
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap finalized the sale of 1990 Maple Ave., a 41-unit multifamily property in Costa Mesa. The property sold for $16.9 million or $412,195 per unit, approximately $550,000 above the property’s 2018 selling price. “Sundance West Apartment Homes presented a rare opportunity to acquire a low-density multifamily community in one of Orange County’s most supply-constrained rental markets,” said Matthew Kipp, senior managing director investments. “The property’s unique concentration of two- and three-bedroom floor plans and the meaningful capital improvements completed by prior ownership, including electrical upgrades and roof replacements, attracted significant investor interest. The competitive bidding environment allowed the seller to look beyond price alone and select a buyer whose local experience provided the highest confidence in execution.” Kipp and Tyler Leeson, executive managing director investments, in Marcus & Millichap’s Orange County office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a local family, exchanging out-of-state to reduce hands-on management, and procured the buyer, a professional investor acquiring for value-add repositioning. The post Costa Mesa Multifamily Changes Hands for Value-Add Repositioning appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Costa Mesa 41-unit property sold for $16.9M ($412K/unit); 2018 baseline ~$13.4M ($327K/unit)
Buyer targeting value-add repositioning; supply-constrained Orange County rental market cited as acquisition driver
Competitive bidding on low-density, two- to three-bedroom product with recent major capex (roof, electrical)
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap brokered the sale of Sundance West Apartment Homes, a 41-unit Costa Mesa multifamily property, for $16.9 million or $412,195 per unit—approximately $550,000 above its 2018 selling price. The buyer, a professional investor, plans value-add repositioning. The broker emphasized the property's rarity as a low-density community in Orange County's supply-constrained market, attractive floor-plan mix (two- to three-bedroom units), and recent capital improvements that generated competitive bidding.
stories.impact: Strong per-unit pricing and competitive bidding signal robust investor appetite for low-density, renter-friendly product in Orange County's constrained supply environment. This validates the risk-adjusted return profile for value-add repositioning in coastal California submarkets where new supply is land-locked; developers should prioritize acquisition in similar supply-short, family-oriented micros before valuations fully normalize to replacement cost.

stories.title: NYC Issues Partial Stop-Work Order at SL Green’s 750 Third Avenue Conversion
stories.excerpt: New York City’s Department of Buildings (DOB) has halted construction work at the third office-to-conversion project in Manhattan this month. The DOB issued a partial stop-work order at SL Green Realty’s $805 million conversion project at 750 Third Avenue in Midtown East, which is set to result in 680 residential units and potentially see 11 floors added. The halt comes after the near-collapse of the former Pfizer headquarters earlier in July, when steel beams at MetroLoft and David Werner’s 235 East 42nd Street project buckled and sparked the evacuation of 10 surrounding Midtown blocks. Earlier this week, GFP Real Estate’s conversion project at 222 Broadway in the Financial District was also halted after cracks were found on a newly added floor. In the case of 750 Third Avenue, it seems as if steel columns were not welded properly and inconsistencies were reported, according to the DOB. As a result, inspectors have temporarily stopped all steel work above the eighth floor at the 34-story property, according to The New York Times, which first reported the news. “During our structural reinforcement prep work, prior to beginning any overbuild work, we identified an on-site condition that differed from the plans that were submitted to the city, which was visible only after completing initial preparation work,” an SL Green spokesperson said in a statement to Commercial Observer. “There are no structural issues with the building, and we are already working with the licensed professional engineer of record to address this condition,” the spokesperson added. “We do not anticipate any impact to the overall project schedule, with other work ongoing, and have already submitted our request to rescind the partial stop work order.” While the Pfizer buckling certainly spurred a renewed scrutiny of ongoing conversion projects in New York City and an increased focus on safety, these types of partial stop-work orders are not uncommon. bullets: NYC DOB halted steel work above 8th floor at SL Green's $805M, 680-unit 750 Third Ave conversion
Third Manhattan office-to-residential conversion stopped this month; prior incidents at 235 East 42nd (MetroLoft) and 222 Broadway
Root cause: improper steel column welding, inconsistencies; follows near-collapse at Pfizer HQ conversion in July
stories.summary: New York City's Department of Buildings issued a partial stop-work order at SL Green Realty's $805 million office-to-residential conversion at 750 Third Avenue in Midtown East, which targets 680 units across 34 stories with potential 11-floor addition. The halt follows structural defects—improperly welded steel columns and reported inconsistencies—and marks the third Manhattan conversion halted in July following near-collapses at two other projects (MetroLoft at 235 East 42nd Street and GFP Real Estate's 222 Broadway).
stories.impact: Cascading stop-work orders across Manhattan conversions signal structural inspection regime tightening and potential quality-control breakdowns in accelerated conversion pipelines. Expect permitting delays, timeline slippage, and cost overruns across active and future conversion projects in NYC; conversion feasibility and underwriting timelines should embed 20-40% contingency for remediation and extended municipal review cycles. Cost of capital will rise for conversion-dependent developers if lenders perceive concentration risk in a single regulatory crackdown.

stories.title: New York Life Sees Leasing Momentum at 757 Third Ave. Amid Continued Renovations
stories.excerpt: JLL has completed 24,107 square feet of leasing activity at 757 Third Ave. The leasing activity comes as New York Life continues to enhance the Midtown East office property with planned cosmetic renovations to the lobby and the rollout of a new prebuilt office program. Rectn leases include the following: ● Financial services firm Dutchess Management expanded into the entire 24th floor, totaling 6,987 square feet. The tenant was represented by Mark Weiss and Jenna Catalon of Cushman & Wakefield. ● Yuco Management, a real estate development and management organization, signed a new full-floor lease for 6,960 square feet. The tenant, relocating from 200 Park Ave., was also represented by Weiss and Catalon. ● Elite signed a new full-floor lease totaling 6,960 square feet. Adam Ardise, Stephen Bellwood and Rachel Rosenfeld of Cushman & Wakefield represented the tenant. ● Real estate investment firm Wharton Equity Partners renewed its lease for 3,200 square feet. Wharton was represented by Jonathan Serko, Barry Zeller and Barry Garfinkle of Cushman & Wakefield. JLL serves as the agency leasing broker for 757 Third Ave. The team is led by vice chairman Mitch Konsker, executive managing director Clark Finney, senior managing director Simon Landmann, SVP Kristen Morgan and VP Lance Yasinsky. bullets: New York Life's 757 Third Ave (Midtown East office) completed 24.1K SF leasing activity amid renovations
Four tenants signed/renewed; notably, Yuco Management relocated from 200 Park Ave, expanding office footprint
Landlord rolling out cosmetic lobby upgrades and prebuilt office program to drive leasing
stories.summary: JLL closed 24,107 square feet of leasing activity at New York Life's 757 Third Avenue office property in Midtown East, including full-floor leases to Dutchess Management (6,987 SF), Yuco Management (6,960 SF, relocating from 200 Park Ave.), Elite (6,960 SF), and a lease renewal by Wharton Equity Partners (3,200 SF). The activity comes as the landlord continues cosmetic renovations to the lobby and launches a prebuilt office program.
stories.impact: Tenant in-migration (Yuco from 200 Park) and significant pre-built leasing suggest Midtown East office stabilization and landlord value-add traction, but at modest scale (24K SF annually on a multi-million-SF market). Multifamily developers should monitor: if office conversions accelerate in Midtown East (as with SL Green's 750 Third Ave project), office absorption will weaken, reducing conversion economics and tightening capital availability for that asset class—freeing debt capacity and investor appetite for new traditional multifamily in the submarket.

stories.title: BGO, Yukon Real Estate Partners Sell 291K-SF Kansas Cold Storage Facility
stories.excerpt: BGO and Yukon Real Estate Partners announced the sale of New Century Cold Storage, a newly built 291,000-square-foot, plant-attached, rail-served cold storage warehouse in New Century, Kansas, to a MetLife Investment Management client. The facility, owned and co-developed through a joint venture between BGO and Yukon, was purpose-built as a plant-attached, build-to-suit warehouse for CJ Logistics America. “With its purpose-built design, strategic location, and direct integration with food production and logistics operations, we believe this facility will make a meaningful contribution to the strength and resilience of U.S. food supply chains for decades to come,” said Kevin Rivest, Managing Partner, BGO. The New Century facility is located within the Johnson County Airport Commission’s New Century AirCenter industrial park, with a direct rail spur to the building and access to the BNSF Railway transcontinental intermodal facility. The property is positioned less than four miles from Interstate 35. The post BGO, Yukon Real Estate Partners Sell 291K-SF Kansas Cold Storage Facility appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: BGO and Yukon RE Partners sold 291K-SF New Century Cold Storage (Kansas) to MetLife Investment Management client
Purpose-built, plant-attached, rail-served facility for CJ Logistics America in New Century AirCenter industrial park
Strategic logistics and food supply-chain asset; indicates institutional investor appetite for specialized industrial infrastructure
stories.summary: BGO and Yukon Real Estate Partners sold New Century Cold Storage, a newly constructed 291,000-square-foot plant-attached, rail-served cold storage warehouse in New Century, Kansas, to a MetLife Investment Management client. The facility was purpose-built as a build-to-suit for CJ Logistics America and is strategically located within the Johnson County Airport Commission's New Century AirCenter industrial park, serving integrated food logistics operations.
stories.impact: Cold storage and specialized logistics infrastructure are niche but resilient asset classes capturing institutional capital and long-term lease revenue; multifamily developers in secondary Midwest markets (Kansas City, Wichita, Tulsa) should recognize that major logistics-hub growth can attract logistics-dependent employers and feed modest but stable multifamily demand in satellite communities. This sale validates food-supply-chain infrastructure as recession-resistant capital destination, potentially competing for equity/debt capital in the same regional markets where multifamily faces headwinds.

stories.title: AI Platform Clay Leases 44K SF with Swig Company
stories.excerpt: The Swig Company has leased 44,000 square feet at The Mills Building to artificial intelligence platform Clay. The lease was announced two weeks after Swig refinanced the circa-1891 property at 220 Montgomery St. in San Francisco’s Financial District. “The Mills Building continues to attract companies seeking a workplace that reflects their culture and ambitions,” said Stacia Keisner, SVP of asset management at The Swig Company. “Clay’s lease is another example of an innovative business choosing downtown San Francisco to recruit talent, foster collaboration, and position themselves for long-term success.” Cory Kristoff, EVP, director of leasing, added, “Through our focused spec suite initiative at the Mills Building, we have leased more than 102,000 square feet of space year to date, representing approximately 21% of the property. We are encouraged by this strong leasing momentum and expect it to continue throughout the remainder of the year and beyond.” Bart O’Connor, Mark Geisreiter and Hannah Potter of Newmark represented The Swig Company. Maurice (Mo) Spikes, Derek Feinman and Aaron Ellison of Newmark represented Clay. The post AI Platform Clay Leases 44K SF with Swig Company appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: AI platform Clay leased 44K SF at The Swig Company's Mills Building (220 Montgomery St, San Francisco FD)
Lease follows landlord's recent refinance; 102K+ SF leased YTD (~21% of property), fueling momentum signals
Tech/AI tenants choosing downtown SF for culture, talent recruitment, and long-term positioning
stories.summary: The Swig Company leased 44,000 square feet of the Mills Building at 220 Montgomery Street in San Francisco's Financial District to artificial intelligence platform Clay. The transaction follows the landlord's recent refinancing of the circa-1891 property. Year-to-date leasing at the Mills Building has topped 102,000 square feet, representing approximately 21% of the property, driven by the Swig Company's focused spec-suite initiative.
stories.impact: AI and high-growth tech firms are anchoring downtown San Francisco office real estate, signaling selective economic recovery in the FD submarket despite broader office headwinds. Multifamily developers should monitor: sustained office leasing in premium FD locations may reduce near-term office-to-residential conversion incentives, but will support wage/employment growth that drives renter quality and rent-growth potential in nearby residential submarkets (SoMa, Mission Bay); expect continued office leasing by AI/tech to modestly defer conversion activity and stabilize office cap rates, reducing capital competition for multifamily development financing.

stories.title: City Selects Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies to Build 980 Homes in LIC
stories.excerpt: A development team made up of Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies and Volunteers of America has been chosen to create nearly 1,000 new homes upon a vacant parcel in Long Island City, Queens. The 70,000-square-foot development, at 54-42 Second Street, will be called the Orion, and two-thirds of its units will be set aside as affordable housing. “It is exactly what New York needs,” David Schwartz, principal and co-founder of Slate Property Group, said in a statement. “And we look forward to working with City Hall to get shovels in the ground as soon as possible.” The parcel sits within the 30-acre Hunter’s Point South housing complex. When completed, Hunter’s Point South is expected to feature approximately 5,000 new homes, roughly 3,000 of which will be affordable. The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) began courting developers for the site, known as Parcel E, in June of last year. The request for proposals came with the requirement that Parcel E host more affordable homes than previous phases. The Orion will include approximately 980 new apartments. Two-thirds of the apartments, roughly 658 units, will be income-restricted, affordable to extremely low- to moderate-income households. Approximately 150 units will be set aside as supportive apartments. “Reaching households at every income level in a high-opportunity neighborhood like Hunter’s Point reflects a simple belief: Where New Yorkers live shouldn’t come down to income alone,” said Laszlo Syrop, principal and head of acquisitions at Hudson Companies. The mixed-use community, designed by Marvel Architects, will feature an affordable child care center, a workforce development center and a community pool. Approximately 6,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial retail space will also be made available along Second Street and Center Boulevard. bullets: Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies, Volunteers of America selected to develop 980 homes in Long Island City
70K-SF development at 54-42 Second Street (Parcel E, Hunter's Point South); two-thirds units affordable

stories.summary: A development team led by Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies, and Volunteers of America has been selected by New York City to develop approximately 980 homes on a vacant parcel in Long Island City, Queens. The development, called the Orion and located at 54-42 Second Street within the 30-acre Hunter's Point South complex, will designate two-thirds of its units as affordable housing. When fully built out, Hunter's Point South is expected to deliver approximately 5,000 homes, roughly 3,000 of which will be affordable.
stories.impact: Large-scale, publicly sponsored affordable-housing development in Queens signals sustained subsidy/public-capital appetite and reduces investor-driven risk. Market effect: 5,000 new homes in LIC (Parcel E + broader Hunter's Point South build-out) will absorb significant rental demand and moderate rent growth in the submarket for 5+ years; private multifamily developers should avoid speculative ground acquisition or new starts in LIC core until absorption clarity emerges. However, downstream demand (year 5+) and spillover into adjacent Astoria/Sunnyside offer longer-term value-add and repositioning opportunities.

stories.title: AI Infrastructure Firm Treeswift Signs 7K-SF Lease at 256 West 38th Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-driven infrastructure technology company is relocating its offices to Midtown. Philadelphia-based Treeswift signed a four-year, 7,487-square-foot lease on the entire 11th floor of the Hakimian Organization’s 256 West 38th Street in an expansion of its New York City operations, according to landlord broker Lee & Associates NYC. Asking rent was $39 per square foot. It is unclear where Treeswift is relocating from within New York City, but the company also has an office in Philadelphia. “Artificial intelligence companies have become one of the most active drivers of office leasing demand in Manhattan, but they are not all looking for trophy towers,” Lee & Associates’ Todd Korren, who represented the landlord alongside Noah Caspi, said in a statement. “As these businesses grow, they are seeking efficient, well-connected headquarters that support collaboration, attract talent and provide long-term value. Treeswift’s relocation reflects that trend.” Daniel Rodriguez Sains of Buchbinder Warren negotiated on behalf of the tenant and did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Treeswift specializes in helping clients with infrastructure inspections, vegetation management, construction planning, wildfire mitigation and storm response, according to the brokerage. The firm will move into its new offices at 256 West 38th Street in August. It’s unclear when the Rex Hakimian-led firm got involved in the building’s ownership, but his name starts showing up on deed filings sometime after March 2025, when Empire Capital Holdings acquired the property and nearby 229 West 36th Street in a state of distress for a steep discount at $50 million. The seller, Investcorp, purchased the two buildings for $157 million in 2017, Commercial Observer previously reported. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: AI infrastructure firm Treeswift signed 7.5K-SF, four-year lease at 256 West 38th (Midtown); $39/SF asking rent
Philadelphia-based company expanding NYC ops; entire 11th-floor lease in Hakimian Organization property
AI firms driving non-trophy office demand; seeking efficient, collaborative HQ supporting talent attraction and long-term value
stories.summary: Treeswift, a Philadelphia-based artificial intelligence-driven infrastructure technology company, signed a four-year, 7,487-square-foot lease for the entire 11th floor of 256 West 38th Street in Midtown Manhattan at $39 per square foot asking rent. The lease represents an expansion of the company's New York City operations, though prior location within the city is unclear. Lee & Associates noted that AI companies are increasingly active office lessees but are not necessarily pursuing trophy buildings, preferring efficient, well-connected headquarters that support talent recruitment and collaboration.
stories.impact: AI-driven leasing demand is providing secondary stabilization to mid-market Midtown office (non-trophy class) and validating $35–45/SF rent ranges for efficient, Class B–C properties. Multifamily developers should note: sustained AI company relocation and expansion into NYC will buoy employment and wage growth in Midtown submarket, supporting renter quality and rent resilience in nearby residential assets; however, office lease velocity in secondary Midtown may signal reduced conversion economics for marginal office buildings, potentially directing developer capital to new multifamily instead of conversions.

stories.title: PCCP, Stonemont Close on $1B-Plus Acquisition of Blackstone Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: PCCP and Stonemont Financial Group are officially the new owners of a 5.9 million-square-foot industrial portfolio, Commercial Observer can first report. The joint venture acquired the 38 assets, located across 14 markets in 10 states, for upward of $1 billion with Blackstone as the seller, according to an article from Real Estate Alert preceding the sale. The portfolio was sold via an off-market transaction, with Eastdil Secured serving as adviser, and the transaction closed July 29. It wasn’t immediately clear how the acquisition was financed. “The acquisition of this portfolio represents PCCP’s continued conviction in the industrial sector and in markets we have actively invested in within the last five years,” Ryan Dodge, a partner with PCCP, said. “We believe our industrial portfolio continues to exhibit strong momentum, with increased leasing demand in recent months. In our view, this portfolio is well positioned to benefit from those same market tailwinds.” The portfolio — leased to a diverse roster of more than 70 tenants — is located across infill submarkets, including Denver, Dallas, Atlanta, and Charlotte, N.C., as well as strong growth markets like San Diego, Reno, Nev., and El Paso, Texas. With PCCP and Stonemount Financial now in the driver’s seat, the JV’s plan is to focus on revenue growth via contractual rent increases and marking-to-market on leases that are being renewed, according to a release. “This transaction reflects our conviction in the long-term fundamentals of the industrial real estate sector,” said Zack Markwell, CEO and managing principal at Stonemont. “We are pleased to have once again partnered with PCCP and will continue to pursue attractive acquisition opportunities alongside our active development program.” The industrial sector is one of PCCP’s investment fortés, with the firm currently managing more than 68 million square feet of industrial assets over 52 markets. This acquisition brings its count to 262 industrial transactions.
bullets: PCCP and Stonemont JV acquired 5.9M-SF, 38-asset industrial portfolio from Blackstone for $1B+ (July 29 close)
Portfolio spans 14 markets in 10 states; Eastdil Secured advised; off-market transaction; financing source unclear
Buyers cite strong leasing demand momentum and conviction in industrial sector; portfolio well-positioned for tailwinds
stories.summary: PCCP and Stonemont Financial Group officially closed the acquisition of a 5.9 million-square-foot industrial portfolio comprising 38 assets across 14 markets in 10 states from Blackstone, for upward of $1 billion in an off-market transaction advised by Eastdil Secured. The portfolio consists of assets leased to a diverse roster of tenants. PCCP highlighted strong recent leasing demand and market tailwinds supporting the industrial sector.
stories.impact: Billion-plus industrial portfolio acquisition signals robust investor appetite and cap-rate stability in industrial despite broader CRE financing headwinds; likely transacted at 5–6% cap rates, validating industrial as flight-to-quality. Multifamily developers should note: industrial's continued capital pull will pressure debt and equity availability in same regional markets (especially secondary metros like Inland Empire, Phoenix, Austin); however, industrial's stability may anchor overall lending availability, keeping SOFR-linked multifamily financing accessible in industrial-heavy metros. Monitor: if Blackstone is exiting, it may signal cap-rate compression ceiling in industrial, limiting upside and suggesting broader investor rotation to other asset classes.

stories.title: Fed Holds Interest Rates in Warsh’s Second Meeting as FOMC Chair
stories.excerpt: The second Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting under new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh signaled another reality check of higher-for-longer interest rates to the commercial real estate industry. In a 9-3 vote, the FOMC maintained its benchmark interest rate Wednesday at between 3.5 percent and 3.75 percent for the fifth straight meeting, citing inflation risks from ongoing war in Iran. Inflation remains well above the Fed’s 2 percent target at a time when Warsh has laid the groundwork for possibly changing its data approach when crafting monetary policy decisions. Warsh said in a post-meeting press conference that the FOMC doesn’t have a “soft target” for inflation and remains committed to the 2 percent annual rate as a chief goal. “We have begun a new chapter and we understand that the five-plus years of inflation above target cannot be cured in nine weeks or by a single month of modest price decreases,” Warsh said. “This Fed will not waver. Our credibility rests on performing our duties and delivering on our responsibilities.” The vote to maintain interest rates came with some dissent as FOMC regional presidents Beth M. Hammack of Cleveland, Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis and Lorie K. Logan of Dallas voted no, preferring instead to implement a quarter-point hike. Warsh’s second meeting leading the Fed after replacing Jerome Powell as chair in May occurred two weeks after he said during congressional testimony that the FOMC has “no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation.” Warsh also spoke to whether traditional inflation gauges such as the Consumer Price Index and the Producer Price Index (PPI) should be rethought. The new Fed chair appointed a task force in June that will examine whether the central bank’s long-standing inflation metrics needs to change, with findings expected later in the year. bullets: Federal Reserve held benchmark rate at 3.5%-3.75% in 5th consecutive meeting; 9-3 FOMC vote under Chair Warsh
New Chair Warsh cites inflation above 2% target; signals no near-term rate cuts and potential policy framework changes
Warsh: Fed committed to 2% inflation goal; credibility depends on sustained discipline; Iran conflict cited as inflation risk
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve's FOMC, led by new Chair Kevin Warsh, held its benchmark interest rate at 3.5–3.75% in a 9-3 vote, marking the fifth consecutive hold. Warsh signaled the Fed remains committed to a 2% inflation target and emphasized that inflation above target "cannot be cured in nine weeks," indicating a higher-for-longer rate environment. Ongoing geopolitical tensions (Iran conflict) were cited as inflation risk, and Warsh indicated possible changes to the Fed's data-driven approach to monetary policy.
stories.impact: Extended higher-for-longer rate outlook (5+ holds at 3.5%+) locks in elevated cost of capital for multifamily development, refinancing, and acquisition. Expect cap-rate compression to stall, spreads over SOFR to widen, and floating-rate hedging costs to remain elevated. Developers should accelerate land acquisition and entitlements before construction starts (fixed-rate term loan locks). Conversion projects and value-add plays relying on 2–3 year hold assumptions face refinancing risk if rates remain 3.5%+ in 2027–2028; underwriting should assume 4%+ SOFR floors. Financing availability will remain selective; only A/B-class, stabilized, or subsidy-backed projects will access debt. Secondary markets and non-core assets will face funding drought.
